title: Worktrees, hooks, signing and large files
summary: The tools that make a professional's Git smoother and safer: several checkouts at once, automatic checks, verified commits, and binaries done right.

steps.title: Worktrees: two branches checked out at once
body: Mid-feature, you must review a PR or fix production. Instead of stashing, check out another branch **in another folder** that shares the same repository:
```bash
git worktree add ../shop-hotfix main      # new folder with main checked out
cd ../shop-hotfix                          # fix, commit, push: same .git, same objects
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../shop-hotfix
Each worktree has its own working tree, index and HEAD; commits, branches and stashes are shared. A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time.
Your half-done feature stays exactly as it was: no stash, no rebuild.

steps.prompt: Why can't you `git switch feature` in a second worktree while `feature` is checked out in the first?
options: Both worktrees would move the same branch with every commit, and one working tree would silently go stale; Git forbids it
steps.explain: Use `git switch --detach feature` there if you only need to look, or create a new branch.

steps.title: Hooks: automatic checks
body: Hooks are scripts Git runs at certain moments, from `.git/hooks/` (or a folder set with `core.hooksPath`, which lets a team commit them):
| Hook | Runs | Typical use |
| `pre-commit` | before the commit is created | format check, lint, **secret scan** |
| `commit-msg` | after the message is written | enforce message format, ticket ids |
| `pre-push` | before pushing | run fast tests |

A hook that exits non-zero **aborts** the operation. `git commit --no-verify` skips client-side hooks, so hooks are a convenience, not a security boundary: anything that must hold is also enforced **server-side** in CI and branch protection.
For .NET teams, tools like Husky.Net install and share hooks; `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` is a common pre-commit.

items: Branch protection: PR + 1 approval to merge to main
Secret scanning on push by the platform

steps.title: Signing commits
body: Anyone can write `user.name = "Your CEO"` in their config; commit authorship is just text. **Signing** proves a commit really came from a key you control:
```bash
git config --global gpg.format ssh                     # sign with an SSH key (simplest)
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true                # sign every commit
git log --show-signature -1
git tag -s v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0"                   # signed tag
Upload the same public key to GitHub/GitLab as a **signing key**, and commits show **Verified**. Many organisations require signed commits on protected branches.

steps.title: Large files and binaries
body: Git keeps **every version of every file forever**, and each clone downloads all of it. A 200 MB video committed ten times is 2 GB in every clone, even after you delete it.
- Keep build outputs, packages and datasets **out** of Git (`.gitignore`; use NuGet feeds, artifact storage).
- For binaries that truly belong with the code (design files, game assets), use **Git LFS**: the repo stores a small pointer file; the content lives on an LFS server and is downloaded on checkout.
```bash
git lfs install
git lfs track "*.psd"           # writes a rule into .gitattributes; commit it
git add .gitattributes design.psd
For huge repos: `git clone --filter=blob:none` (partial clone: fetch file contents on demand) and `git sparse-checkout` (only some folders).

steps.title: A pre-commit secret scanner

build.unlocks: gitkit scan now stops secrets before they are committed.
build.title: Pre-commit secret scanner
transform: // Your passing code from the code-dojo Git track.

prompt: > This piece becomes `gitkit scan` and is wired in as a real `pre-commit` hook by the gitkit tool. The next step does the same job the quick way, as a shared shell hook in a real repository.

Write `Scan(Dictionary<string, string> files)` for a `pre-commit` hook. It returns one finding per matching line, as `path:line: rule`, files sorted by path (ordinal), lines in order (1-based), rules in this order:
A line can produce several findings. Use `System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex.IsMatch`.
solution: var rules = new (string Name, string Pattern)[]
foreach (var (path, content) in files.OrderBy(f => f.Key, StringComparer.Ordinal))
hints: Keep the rules in an array of `(Name, Pattern)` tuples so the order is fixed.
Split each file on `\n` and loop with an index for the line number.
Use verbatim strings (`@"..."`) for the regexes.
template: Dojo.Eq("finds the secrets", new List<string> { "appsettings.json:2: password", "deploy.sh:1: AWS access key", "id_rsa:1: private key" }, Scan(dojoFiles));
Dojo.Eq("clean code passes", new List<string>(), Scan(new() { ["a.cs"] = "var passwordLength = 12;" }));

steps.title: A shared pre-commit hook
prompt: Your team wants every clone of `~/shop` to refuse commits that add an AWS access key id (`AKIA` followed by 16 capital letters or digits).

1. Write the hook as `.githooks/pre-commit` **inside the repo**, so it is shared: it must exit 1 with a message when the staged changes add such a key, and 0 otherwise. `git diff --cached -U0` shows the staged lines; added lines start with `+`.
2. Make it executable and point Git at the folder: `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`.
3. Commit the hook on the current branch. Do **not** commit the half-done `src/Wishlist.cs` change.
The check clones your repo, sets `core.hooksPath` like a teammate would, and tries a commit with a key and one without.

checks.name: the hook blocks a key and allows a normal commit
checks.fail: The shared hook is not right yet.

checks.name: the half-done Wishlist change is still uncommitted
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && grep -q 'half done' src/Wishlist.cs && ! git show HEAD:src/Wishlist.cs | grep -q 'half done'
checks.fail: `src/Wishlist.cs` should keep its uncommitted edit. Commit with `git add .githooks` and `git commit`, not `-a`.

hints: The test inside the hook: `git diff --cached -U0 | grep -qE '^\+.*AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}'`.

`mkdir -p .githooks`, then write the file with `printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/sh' 'if git diff --cached -U0 | grep -qE "^\+.*AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}"; then' '  echo "pre-commit: an AWS access key id is staged" >&2' '  exit 1' 'fi' > .githooks/pre-commit`.
`chmod +x .githooks/pre-commit`, `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`, `git add .githooks`, `git commit -m "Add a shared pre-commit hook against AWS keys"`.
solution: printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/sh' 'if git diff --cached -U0 | grep -qE "^\+.*AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}"; then' '  echo "pre-commit: an AWS access key id is staged" >&2' '  exit 1' 'fi' > .githooks/pre-commit
git commit -m "Add a shared pre-commit hook against AWS keys"
steps.explain: Hooks in `.git/hooks` are never cloned, so a team keeps them in the repo and each clone opts in with `core.hooksPath` (or a tool such as pre-commit, Husky or Lefthook does it for them). Hooks are a convenience, not a control: `git commit --no-verify` skips them. The real guard against leaked keys is server-side: GitHub push protection and secret scanning.

steps.title: A hotfix in a second worktree
prompt: You are in the middle of `feature/wishlist` in `~/shop`, with an uncommitted, half-done edit. An urgent bug arrives: the VAT rate on `main` is `0.12m` and must be `0.21m`.
Without stashing or committing your half-done work:
1. Add a second worktree at `~/shop-hotfix` on a **new** branch `hotfix/vat` started from `main`.
2. There, fix the rate in `src/Vat.cs` and commit it as `Fix VAT rate`.
Your feature worktree must be exactly as you left it.

checks.name: ~/shop-hotfix is a worktree on hotfix/vat
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && git worktree list --porcelain | grep -qx "worktree $HOME/shop-hotfix" && test "$(git -C ~/shop-hotfix branch --show-current)" = hotfix/vat
checks.fail: `git worktree list` should show `~/shop-hotfix` on `hotfix/vat`. `git worktree add -b hotfix/vat ~/shop-hotfix main` makes both.

checks.name: hotfix/vat has the fix on top of main
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && test "$(git log -1 --format=%s hotfix/vat)" = 'Fix VAT rate' && git show hotfix/vat:src/Vat.cs | grep -q '0.21m' && test "$(git rev-parse hotfix/vat^)" = "$(git rev-parse main)"
checks.fail: `hotfix/vat` should be `main` plus one commit, `Fix VAT rate`, that sets `0.21m`.

checks.name: the feature worktree is untouched
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && test "$(git branch --show-current)" = feature/wishlist && grep -q 'half done' src/Wishlist.cs && test -z "$(git stash list)"
checks.fail: `~/shop` should still be on `feature/wishlist` with the half-done edit uncommitted, and nothing stashed.

hints: `git worktree add -b <new-branch> <path> <start>` creates the branch and checks it out in a new folder.
`git commit -am "Fix VAT rate"` there. `git worktree list` from either folder shows both.
steps.explain: A worktree is a second checkout sharing one object store: no second clone, no stash juggling, and your editor and build output in `~/shop` stay put. When the hotfix is merged, `git worktree remove ~/shop-hotfix` cleans up (and `git worktree prune` forgets folders you deleted by hand).
